Mr. Speaker, a few days ago I asked a question of the Minister of Supply and Services concerning the Auditor General's report and the 14 points that he put forth touching on the security of our computers, the information that we have in the memory bank of all our computers. The answer that the minister gave me obviously did not suit me, which is why I am here today. I could not let this go by without bringing to his attention some very important facts about the whole matter.
I do not pretend in any way to be an expert in this field; far from it. It is highly complex and I know it is a very expensive system to operate. You do not need a college degree to realize the way the computer systems are set up with the memory banks that we have, the data base, and all the rest of it is highly complex and very expensive.
However, I have to draw to the attention of the government some points that are very important. After I heard the minister, I was in touch with a gentleman who is a recognized expert in the field. Of course, we looked at this very objectively and as you will see, Mr. Speaker, from the points I am bringing out, it is standard procedure in a way.
Adjournment Debate
To begin with, I must say that after looking at the Auditor General's report, there is an element of neglect here, negligence if I may say so; negligence because it has been over five years that the Auditor General has been bringing attention to the fact that with all the data banks we have, it could literally cripple the operation of the government overnight if some kind of accident was to occur. Not necessarily all services could be affected, but a great number could be very much affected. It could cripple our whole system and it could be extremely expensive to get it back on track.
The reason why there is this negligence is the fact that there has been such a low priority given to the security aspect of our data banks. We have to remember today that more and more of our computer whizzes are out there and we are dealing with a lot of anonymous people who are becoming more and more capable with this computer age.
One term that the expert gave me was what he called the logical entrance whereby some people can actually get into a government data base, change the information that is in the data base on a particular individual, add information that is not there and should not be there obviously, or else simply take all the information in the data base and put it in their own memory bank. Needless to say, there is a question of confidentiality at play here and there is reason to be concerned. Those are the things that can happen, and it is a fact. I did not invent all this. This is a fact.
The expert said to me basically as it stands right now, it is as if we gave the keys to anybody passing by who knows how to operate a door. Therefore, with the lack of security we have, it would not be difficult to break into a lot of our data base information. That is factual. You would have to admit that if that is the case, it is not a very good management principle.
Look at our financial institutions. They manipulate a tremendous amount of information, highly confidential and they have taken upon themselves to have the best security possible. Still they manage to make money.
Obviously, there is a set standard that could be set up to protect the data bases that we have in the government; very important.

Adjournment Debate

Mr. Speaker, after demonstrating the negligence in this area, and I am not saying the government is fully responsible, because the problem may go back ten years, but for the past five years the Auditor General has said the situation cannot go on like this.
I spoke to an expert, and I told him: I don't want a complex answer, I want to keep it very simple, but according to you-he had read the Auditor General's report and he was aware there was some lack of security- he made the following suggestions:

To begin with, he said we should have set standards of security. This could be done over a period of five years. Set standards, followed by a workable plan not too far in the future but within a reasonable amount of time. A work plan.
That should be approached, and it should be looked into immediately by our senior management in the government, especially Treasury Board because it holds the strings.
There is no doubt that it could be expensive business. Nevertheless, there is a work plan that could be out. We could do it over a period of time because security is the cost of doing business.
Finally, we have to remember that all this information is an asset. All the information is government asset. There is the old saying in French:

"Celui qui possede Vinformation possede le pouvoir".
Finally, Mr. Speaker, and very briefly, I do not think we should criticize without offering alternatives, but we must have a plan and deal with the problem before mistakes are made that may cost us very dearly and cause Canadians to have some very serious doubts about the security of our information.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Monique Tardif (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Supply and Services):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity today to respond to the question put by the hon. member for Gatineau-La Lievre about government information systems.

Mr. Speaker, in response to the concern raised by the Auditor General in the past year, the department has taken the issue very seriously and moved to create the information management sector within the department.
This sector oversees the secure handling and storage of the government's data banks. We have moved to create a secure regime. This is not mentioned in the report.

Mr. Speaker, the security of our computer systems is extremely important to the Department of Supply and Services and to all government departments and agencies. I can assure the House and Canadians that very strict security measures have been taken to keep any risk or damage to our systems to an absolute minimum.
Increasingly, detailed emergency plans have been provided to ensure maintenance of the government's daily operations, in case of computer failure.
Mr. Speaker, I fully understand the hon. member's concerns. Computers now play an important role in our daily lives, and we are increasingly aware of the potential damage that could be caused by pirates and viruses.
However, although I understand his concerns, I think the hon. member should realize that security measures are in place to prevent any violation of the confidentiality and integrity of the full range of information processed by the government.
Mr. Speaker, as was previously mentioned in this House by the Minister of Supply and Services, there are regular security checks, not only of computers in government offices but also in the offices of businesses that deal with the government. Furthermore, as the minister also pointed out, only very low level intelligence or information that represents a very low security risk may be processed outside government offices.
Consequently, Mr. Speaker, I have no hesitation in stating before this House and before all Canadians that both government facilities and those of our suppliers are checked regularly and that security levels are maintained. Mr. Speaker, perhaps the fact that there has never been any serious damage to our systems reflects the effectiveness of our security policy and its successful implementation throughout our government services.

subtopic: THE CITIZENS' FORUM ON THE FUTURE OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, thank you for recognizing me on a current issue of great concern to Canadians. I am referring of course to the new commission, the Citizens' Forum, chaired by Mr. Keith Spicer. Made up of twelve members, this commission will be listening to the comments of Canadians on the future of our country.
In the House last Tuesday, November 5, I put a question to the Deputy Prime Minister to find out whether or not additional people would be appointed to the commission, the better to represent all Canadians who, like me for instance, felt somewhat left out in the make-up of the famous commission.
As you may recall, Mr. Speaker, in one of my questions to the government I enquired if there was room for people north of the 60th parallel, Canadian men and women who we all know are very ably represented here by my colleagues from Nunatsiaq and Western Arctic. I also asked: Is there room for francophones outside Quebec? Is there room on that commission to listen to the million Canadians who live outside Quebec and whose mother tongue happens to be French, an official language of this country? I also asked the Deputy Prime Minister if we could expect to see a wider spectrum of representatives of ethnic groups, because I think that is important when close to one third of our country is made up of new immigrants, Canadians who represent a rather large variety of world cultures and languages, so as I said I think it is important that these people as well be consulted about the future of this country. I was told that no one else could be added to the membership of the Citizens' Forum.
Well, the very next Sunday, before the National Convention of Italian Canadians in Toronto, the Prime Minister said that there might be room for additional appointments. I was rather surprised because of what I had been told a few days before. Yet, the Prime Minister had said: "Yes, there is room for additional appointments."
Later on, we learned that Chairman Spicer himself had been reported as confirming the statement made by the Deputy Prime Minister and the Secretary of State the previous day that there would be no new members.
Adjournment Debate
So, my question tonight to the Parliamentary Secretary is this: Are there going to be additional appointments to the Citizens' Forum? Could we have a clear, straightforward and precise answer to this question?
Second, how come the commission will not report to Parliament? It was a very specific question. Does the appointment of this commission means also that the government has abandonned its plans for reform? The House will remember that following the Oka incidents last Summer, the government had made the firm commitment to set up a commission to look into and possibly settle the land claims of our native citizens. Now we hear that the government has decided to put these concerns on the backbumer while the Spicer Commission is sitting. My question to the Parliamentary Secretary is this: Is it true that the government is going to set aside these concerns which he feels are justified, for an indefinite period.
Third question: Is this new Spicer Commission a substitute for the commission this Tory government has promised on native affairs? We want to hear a straightforward yes or no. This way, the Natives and I will know where we stand.
Also, could the parliamentary secretary indicate if, with the setting up of this commission, we can expect in this country a reform of our institutions? For instance, would it be possible for the Senate, a major concern for a number of Canadians, to become a better Senate, the elected one we want, or will we still have to wait until the commission has completed its study?
Mr. Speaker, these questions stem from the appointe-ment of this commission. I would not want the parliamentary secretary to answer all my questions tonight, but I should be quite satisfied if he could answer at least a couple of them.

speakeroldname: Mr. Len Gustafson (Parliamentary Secretary to Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
subtopic: THE CITIZENS' FORUM ON THE FUTURE OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to respond to the address by the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier.
A suggestion is being made that the advisory group be expanded by the addition of members from the north, from ethnic communities and from francophone minorities outside of Quebec. Perhaps from other groups as well.

Adjournment Debate
I am sorry to have to say that the question betrays a failure to understand the innovative process the government has launched. The hon. member seems to have missed the point.
The key is that it is a citizens' forum in fact as well as in name. The word "citizen", and I will repeat "citizen", cannot be stressed too strongly. The forum is not intended to be an arena where elite representatives can debate once again among themselves. It is something quite different, a place where individual Canadians can speak out and engage in a dialogue among themselves. It is a place where individual Canadians can contribute their insight and their dreams in mapping a new national consensus.
As the Prime Minister pointed out when he announced in this House on November 1, the forum is an initiative for the people and of the people. I repeat, as the Prime Minister said, for the people and of the people.
This means that the 11 members of the advisory group are not there to represent a particular group. That is not the basis on which it is formed. They were chosen as distinguished Canadians who are committed to helping their fellow citizens to chart the path of Canada's future. This is why they are members of the advisory group. I would add that it is interesting that members selected on their basis of many ways do reflect, individually and collectively, Canada's diversity.
Their job is to listen and to facilitate a productive dialogue, not to defend the barricades on behalf of linguistic, ethnic, regional or other blocs. When they speak, they speak as Canadians sensitive to our unity as much as to our diversity.
The Prime Minister did indicate over the weekend that he was prepared to consider expanding the advisory group. He would listen carefully to any recommendations from Mr. Spicer that additional members be appointed. Surely, that is a normal procedure. If Mr. Spicer came back and said "We need more people", the Prime Minister would be duty bound to give that very serious consideration.
Canadians would expect that the Prime Minister do whatever was necessary to make the citizens' forum work. Mr. Spicer has now said publicly that he does not foresee a need for additional members. He points out, as I have tried to do, that the advisers do not hear as specific representatives of their community, but more as good listeners and communicators. I want to emphasize
as good listeners. It was quoted in The Citizen November 7, so the question is now purely academic.
It should be clear for all that I have said-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to return to the issues I raised with the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development on September 24. One of those issues was the land question of Oka-Kanesatake.
I had asked the minister that day about the status of the land which the government had acquired over the summer which was supposed to be transferred to the Mohawk people of Kanesatake. At the time I asked the question the land which had been bought was still in the hands of the government. My point, then, was that it has not yet been turned over to the Mohawk people. My point is still valid. The land still has not been turned over to the Mohawk people of Kanesatake.
Only two days ago, the Minister of Indian and Northern Affairs announced he was prepared to begin negotiations with the Kanesatake Mohawk negotiating committee. We, on this side of the House, welcome that announcement. It has been a long time coming.
As I have said on earlier occasions in this House, we wish the land issue at Kanesatake could have been settled without the violence we witnessed this summer. We wish the government would have made such an announcement in the spring of this year. Had it done so, the whole ugly episode of arms and soldiers in Oka and Kahnawake could have been avoided.
Nevertheless, at least some kind of process is beginning now; and I stress beginning. There is a long way to go with these negotiations. Land, housing, economic development, community infrastructure and self-government are among the agenda items.
We want these negotiations to start soon. We want them to go well. We hope that the government will conduct itself in these negotiations with fairness and justice. We want a just and fair resolution of this issue for the Mohawk people of Kanesetake. We want a just and fair settlement of the entire land claim of the Mohawk people of Kanesatake, which, as the government knows, encompasses much more than the 97 acres the government acquired this summer.

My question to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development on September 24 dealt as well with the government's general approach and attitude to aboriginal issues and aboriginal rights. I asked how we could be assured that the government would follow through on its promised aboriginal agenda, given its record of broken promises and unfulfilled obligations.
In recent days, doubt and confusion have surrounded the government's commitment to aboriginal issues. On September 25, the Prime Minister announced his government's new aboriginal agenda. That agenda, in his words, has four main pillars: land claims, the economic and social conditions on reserves, the relationship between aboriginal peoples and governments, and concerns of Canada's aboriginal peoples in contemporary Canadian life.
On November 1, the Prime Minister announced the establishment of the Citizens' Forum on Canada's Future, headed by Keith Spicer. There were no representatives from the northern territories appointed to the commission. Is it because, as the hon. member pointed out earlier, that this was a forum of distinguished Canadians? Is it because they could not find distinguished Canadians in the north? That is basically what he is saying.
The government has not listened to the appeals from this side of the House and from the north to appoint a northern resident to this commission. Once again, the north has been ignored. As I pointed out, the Prime Minister was quite prepared to consider it because he was under pressure from a certain ethnic group after apologising about past wrongs.
This past weekend, the government's federal-provincial relations minister said there will be no royal commission on aboriginal issues while the Citizen's Forum is at work. This royal commission had been promised to aboriginal people last June by the Prime Minister to try and entice their support for the Meech Lake Accord. When the accord died, so did the promised royal commission. Now it is clear that it will not happen, at least while the Citizen's Forum is at work.
Adjournment Debate
Despite the government's promise to accelerate the settlement of land claims, yesterday it closed the door on most of the Dene and Metis in the Northwest Territories. They then got into pressure tactics because the Minister of Indian and Northern Affairs says that a freeze on development of land in the north Slave region will be lifted at the end of January. The development freeze was made to avoid jeopardizing the final land selection process. As soon as he announced that there would be not be any more negotiations, that land freeze was lifted. If that is not pressure tactics, then what is?
The government refuses to change its claims policy so that aboriginal people would no longer have to extinguish their aboriginal rights to achieve a settlement.
The government must recognize that there are serious problems with its comprehensive claims policy. These problems are not going to go away just because the government has agreed to negotiate more claims at a time, or because more resources will be devoted to these negotiations.
On this side of the House, we welcomed the Prime Minister's commitment to accelerate claim negotiations and devote more effort and resources to their settlement. But we were, and remain, skeptical about the extent of the commitment. We have heard such promises before. We have seen them broken. Not all the obstacles toward fair and just settlements have been removed.
The aspirations of aboriginal people in this country will continue to be frustrated unless the government shows, through real and positive action, that it is prepared to relinquish its control over the lives of aboriginal people.
Just to show the attitude of some of the members on the government side, two days ago the hon. member for Chateauguay announced that he was disappointed that the government paid $5.2 million to buy 39 hectares to give to the 750 Mohawks of the Kanesatake settlement. I agree that they should not have paid $5.2 million to the town. They should have given the land to the Mohawks, as well as pay $5.2 million for the use of that land over the last number of years.
This same hon. member also said: "The Indians are asking for three-quarters of Canada". I think that is being pretty generous.

Adjournment Debate

speakeroldname: Mr. Len Gustafson (Parliamentary Secretary to Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in response to the hon. member's words this evening, events of the past summer in Kanesatake have forced all Canadians to think deeply about their country and its future and about the values that we share as Canadians. We need to understand why things went wrong, and why desperate measures were taken to draw attention to issues that should have been settled through negotiations.
We have in our country a tradition of discussion, negotiation and compromise, a process that respects the views of others and recognizes that no one side has a monopoly on justice and virtue.
I want to remind members of the action that the government has taken recently. On Tbesday, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development announced that he has agreed to commence negotiations with the committee, composed of the coalition of Kanesatake community groups and, additionally, had invited the band council to name a representative to the community negotiating committee. This is a fulfilment of a commitment made during the crisis at Oka this summer. The minister met with the Honourable Christos Sirros, his Quebec counterpart, on November 2. Mr. Sirros indicated that Quebec is prepared to commence negotiations with the Kanesatake representatives and to express his willingness to allow representatives of the parish and municipality of Oka to be a part of the provincial negotiating contingent.
The federal government believes strongly that the community of Kanesatake, as a whole, must be a part of the decision-making and therefore a priority of the negotiators will be to develop a ratification process. Clearly, any agreement reached by the negotiators will be taken to the community for approval.
Items on the agenda will likely include the development of a unified land base for the Kanesatake community, including final disposition of the recently acquired 97 acres; the provision of housing, necessary community infrastructure and economic development at Kanesatake; the grievance of the Kanesatake Mohawks related to the former lands of the seigneuiy of the Lake of Two Mountains at Oka and, in particular, to the so-called "common lands"; and the development of self-government agreement with the Mohawks of Kanesatake.
The minister has introduced the chief federal negotiator, Bernard Roy, to convene the first meeting of the negotiators at the earliest possible date.
We are hopeful that the negotiations will lead to the agreements leading to peace and prosperity for the community of Kanesatake.
